\chapter{Black, White, Red, and Blue}
\label{ch:spanish-black-white-red-blue}
\hlchaptermodality{44}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name black, white, red and blue in Spanish and say which of them Spanish borrowed rather than inherited.}

Say negro, blanco, rojo and azul, then sort them by origin: negro inherited from Latin, blanco traditionally linked to the Germanic Visigoths, rojo a cousin of English red by a different Latin branch, and azul carried in from Arabic lāzaward.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[negro, blanco]{negro, blanco — two colours, and one of their histories}

\label{lesson:ES-C22-negro-blanco}



\begin{quote}
Two colours you can put to work immediately. One of them has the most ordinary history imaginable. The other does not — which is why it gets its own lesson next.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{negro} (\textquotedblleft{}black\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{niger}. Nothing surprising: the same Latin root gives English \textbf{denigrate} (\textquotedblleft{}to blacken someone's name\textquotedblright{}) and the rest of the Romance family's words for black — French \emph{noir}, Italian \emph{nero}, Portuguese \emph{negro}. Latin's word for black stayed put, in every daughter language.

Hold that in mind as the baseline. It is what a colour word normally does.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{The two words in use}
\textbf{blanco} (\textquotedblleft{}white\textquotedblright{}) is the pair to it: \emph{el gato negro}, \emph{el gato blanco}. Both behave like any Spanish adjective — they follow the noun and agree with it (\emph{la casa blanca}).

But hear what you would have expected and did not get. Latin's word for white was \textbf{albus}, and by the \emph{negro} pattern Spanish \textquotedblleft{}white\textquotedblright{} should be something like \emph{albo}. It is not. Where \textbf{blanco} actually came from — and what became of \emph{albus} — is the next lesson.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}negro, blanco\textquotedblright{}
  \item with a noun — \textquotedblleft{}el gato negro, la casa blanca\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}negro\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}denigrate\textquotedblright{} — the \emph{niger} root
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say black and white. (\emph{Negro, blanco}.) Where does \emph{negro} come from, and what English word shares it? (Latin \textbf{niger} — \emph{denigrate}.) What would you have expected Spanish's \textquotedblleft{}white\textquotedblright{} to be, given Latin \emph{albus}? (Something like \emph{albo} — and it isn't. That is next lesson's puzzle.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[blanco from \emph{blank}]{blanco — the colour Spanish did not inherit}

\label{lesson:ES-C22-blanco-germanico}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Negro} came straight down from Latin, like almost every other everyday word you have met. \textbf{Blanco} did not come down at all. It walked in.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item negro, blanco — the two colour words.
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{blanco} comes from \textbf{Germanic *blank} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{shining, gleaming}.\textquotedblright{} It is a \textbf{loan}, traditionally attributed to contact with the \textbf{Visigoths}, the Germanic people who ruled Spain for centuries after Rome collapsed.

Be careful how firmly you hold that last part: no surviving Gothic text actually preserves this word, so the Visigothic route is a \textbf{plausible traditional account}, not a documented one. What \emph{is} well attested is the parallel case next door — \textbf{French} took the very same Germanic word (\emph{blanc}) from a \textbf{different} Germanic people, the \textbf{Franks}. Two Romance sisters, the same borrowed word for white, two separate borrowings.

Why would a borrowed word beat Latin's own? Because \emph{*blank} was not a pale word: it meant \textbf{bright, gleaming}. Colour terms lose out to vivid ones all the time — English's own \emph{bright} is doing the same job in \textquotedblleft{}bright white.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Latin's white did not vanish. It stopped being the \textbf{everyday} word and survived in corners:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{meaning} & \textbf{the white inside} \\
\midrule
\textbf{alba} & dawn & the sky going \emph{white} \\
\emph{albo} (rare, poetic) & white, pale & a fossil, mostly literary now \\
\emph{álbum} (Eng. \emph{album}) & album & a \emph{blank white} tablet \\
\emph{albino} & albino & white-skinned \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

That is the normal fate of a displaced word: not death, but retreat into technical and poetic corners. \emph{El alba} is still every Spanish speaker's word for dawn.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the pairing — \textquotedblleft{}negro from Latin, blanco from Germanic\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}el alba\textquotedblright{} — dawn — and hear the old Latin white inside it
  \item \textquotedblleft{}blanco\textquotedblright{} then French \textquotedblleft{}blanc\textquotedblright{} — the same loan, twice over
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does \textbf{blanco} come from, and what did it mean? (\textbf{Germanic *blank}, \textquotedblleft{}shining\textquotedblright{} — traditionally linked to the Visigoths, though not directly attested.) Which other language borrowed the same word, from whom? (\textbf{French} \emph{blanc}, from the \textbf{Franks}.) Where did Latin's \emph{albus} end up? (In \textbf{alba} \textquotedblleft{}dawn,\textquotedblright{} \emph{álbum}, \emph{albino} — no longer the everyday colour word.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[rojo]{rojo — the same family as \emph{red}, by a different branch}

\label{lesson:ES-C22-rojo}



\begin{quote}
So far the sorting has been simple: \emph{negro} inherited, \emph{blanco} borrowed. \textbf{Rojo} needs a third box — inherited, yes, but not from the word you would guess.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{rojo} (\textquotedblleft{}red\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{russus}, an everyday, expressive Latin word for red. That is a \textbf{different specific Latin word} from the one behind French \emph{rouge} ($\leftarrow$ \textbf{rubeus}). Latin had several reds and the daughter languages did not all pick the same one.

Both \emph{russus} and \emph{rubeus}, though, descend from the very same ancient root: PIE \emph{\textbf{h\textsubscript{1}rewd\textsuperscript{h}-}} — which is also the root of English \textbf{red}, \textbf{rust}, \textbf{ruddy}, and of Latin \emph{ruber} itself (English \textbf{rubric}, once written in red ink).

So \emph{rojo}, \emph{rouge} and \emph{red} are \textbf{cousins}, not copies: three descendants of one very old family, arriving by three different branches. Nobody borrowed this one from anybody.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}rojo\textquotedblright{}
  \item the cousins — \textquotedblleft{}rojo · rouge · red\textquotedblright{}, three branches, one root
  \item the three so far — \textquotedblleft{}negro inherited, blanco borrowed, rojo cousin\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \textbf{rojo} from the same Latin word as French \emph{rouge}? (\textbf{No} — \emph{rojo} $\leftarrow$ \emph{russus}, \emph{rouge} $\leftarrow$ \emph{rubeus}.) Are they related at all? (\textbf{Yes} — cousins, via the shared PIE root \emph{h\textsubscript{1}rewd\textsuperscript{h}-}, which also gives English \textbf{red}.) Next: the one colour in this chapter that came from outside Europe entirely.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[azul]{azul — a stone from Afghanistan, in your everyday vocabulary}

\label{lesson:ES-C22-azul}



\begin{quote}
Three colours in, three different histories: inherited, borrowed from a neighbour, inherited by a different branch. The fourth comes from outside the Indo-European family altogether.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{azul} (\textquotedblleft{}blue\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ Arabic \textbf{\esar{لازورد}} (\emph{lāzaward}), \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{lapis lazuli}\textquotedblright{} — the deep blue stone, mined for centuries in what is now Afghanistan and ground into the most expensive pigment in the medieval world. Spanish picked the word up during the centuries of Arabic-speaking rule in Iberia (\textbf{al-Andalus}). English has the same source at one more remove, in \textbf{azure}, and the stone keeps its own name: \textbf{lazuli}.

So Spanish's word for blue is, underneath, the name of a \textbf{rock} — which is common for blue. Blue is the last basic colour term most languages acquire, and when they do, they usually name it after the thing that was reliably that colour.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Here is the contrast worth keeping. \textbf{French} has \emph{azur} too — but only as a \textbf{secondary, poetic} word (the sky's blue, the \emph{Côte d'Azur}); its everyday blue is the Germanic loan \emph{bleu}. In \textbf{Spanish} it is the reverse: \textbf{azul is the plain, unremarkable, everyday word}, with no Germanic rival competing for the job at all.

Same borrowed word, two languages, opposite outcomes — a reminder that where a word came from tells you nothing about how ordinary it now feels.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all four — \textquotedblleft{}negro, blanco, rojo, azul\textquotedblright{}
  \item sort them — \textquotedblleft{}negro inherited, blanco Germanic, rojo cousin of red, azul Arabic\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}azul\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}azure\textquotedblright{} — the same lapis lazuli
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Name the four colours and sort them by origin. (\emph{Negro} — Latin \emph{niger}; \emph{blanco} — Germanic \emph{*blank}; \emph{rojo} — Latin \emph{russus}, cousin of \emph{red}; \emph{azul} — Arabic \emph{lāzaward}.) What did \emph{lāzaward} actually name? (\textbf{Lapis lazuli}, the stone.) How does \emph{azul}'s role differ from French \emph{azur}'s? (\textbf{Azul is Spanish's everyday blue}; French's \emph{azur} is only poetic, with \emph{bleu} doing the daily work.)
\end{tcolorbox}
